As a public benefit corporation, we are required to balance the pecuniary interests of our stockholders, the best interests of those materially affected by our conduct, and the specific public benefit purpose identified in our amended and restated certificate of incorporation: the responsible development and maintenance of advanced AI for the long-term benefit of humanity. We created our Long-Term Benefit Trust (the “LTBT”) to help ensure that Anthropic, PBC is managed in a manner that responsibly balances its goals as a public benefit corporation. The LTBT is intended to operate as an independent body of financially disinterested trustees with expertise in AI safety, national security, public policy, and social enterprise. Through a special class of common stock, Class T common stock, the LTBT generally has the authority to elect and remove the Class T directors, who together will constitute a majority of the authorized members of our board of directors. Our Class T common stock does not otherwise have voting rights with respect to matters submitted to stockholders generally and has no economic rights. Inference occurs each time a user or agent interacts with an SI system. “ **interleaved thinking** ” refers to a capability whereby an SI model interposes discrete reasoning steps between successive tool calls within a single response, rather than confining its reasoning to a single planning phase at the outset. 

“ **interpretability** ” refers to research into how and why SI models produce specific outputs, with the goal of making model behavior more transparent and verifiable, especially in high-stakes applications. 

“ **knowledge work** ” refers to complex cognitive work and related professional activities, including obtaining, producing, analyzing, and communicating information through tasks such as coding, drafting analyses, synthesizing research, building financial models, and managing and automating documents and workflows. “ **LLMs** ” refer to large language models, or SI models trained primarily on large datasets to understand and generate natural language and computer code. 

“ **mechanistic interpretability** ” refers to a subfield of interpretability research focused on reverseengineering the internal computations of neural networks. Rather than inferring model behavior from inputs and outputs alone, mechanistic interpretability seeks to identify the specific features and circuits within a model that give rise to its behavior with the goal of making model reasoning auditable at the mechanism level and detecting failure modes, including deceptive or unsafe behavior, that may not surface in standard testing.

##### **_Our Core Advantages_** 
_Mission & Focus_ . All of our efforts are guided by a singular focus on our mission. This focus enables us to concentrate talent, research, and compute investment on the highest-value work for humanity and to avoid conflicting priorities. Achieving our mission means the world gains the enormous benefits of frontier intelligence while mitigating the most significant risks, and we believe this requires safety and capability to advance together. 

_Talent & Culture._ Our mission and focus enable us to attract and retain world-class talent, including researchers and engineers who want their work to shape a better future. We also have a culture that promotes a low-ego, truth-seeking environment, where frontier capability and safety are mutually reinforcing. We believe our culture has driven our talent density as we have scaled.

##### **_The Importance of Safety and Ethical Behavior_** 
While the potential benefits of super intelligence are extraordinary, its rapid advancement will impact the economy and society in ways that could create significant disruption, particularly if these technologies are not developed and deployed responsibly. For example, bad actors have already conducted high-profile cyberattacks using frontier model capabilities to discover vulnerabilities, generate malware, and evade detection tools; other risks associated with misuse, including in the domain of biology, could result in even greater harm. Frontier models deployed at scale also have the potential to concentrate power and wealth both within and between countries in ways that could erode trust, harm society, and destabilize the geopolitical order. Misaligned models could corrupt institutional decision-making or cause large-scale harm through autonomous actions that are not visible or understandable to their users and operators. We believe that companies at the frontier must invest in safety and alignment to help ensure the responsible diffusion of this technology. We also believe that safety, alignment, and ethical behavior resonate particularly strongly with enterprises, where rigorous safeguards, predictable model behavior, and demonstrable accountability have become decisive criteria in selecting a partner for mission-critical workloads.

We believe the diffusion of super intelligence through the global economy represents one of the largest opportunities in history to improve how humans live and work, and it is just beginning. In our view, the world has only begun to use the capabilities of today’s frontier models, and the gap between what Claude can do and how broadly it is used represents one of our largest growth opportunities, alongside continued advances at the frontier. Claude’s capabilities have evolved significantly in recent years, and we expect they will continue advancing rapidly. This will lead not only to an expanding addressable market, but also to an expanding scope of impact on the world. We aim to ensure that impact is as positive as possible. Our core advantages, the speed and scale of enterprise adoption of Claude, and our unprecedented financial model enable us to continue investing aggressively to build a future enabled by this technology that benefits humanity broadly. _Balancing Safety and Commercial Objectives_ . Our commitment to AI safety requires us to make difficult judgments that balance safety considerations against commercial objectives, competitive pressures, and stakeholder expectations. We often make judgment calls with respect to when we determine a model is safe enough to release and which capabilities to develop or restrict. For example, in April 2026, we initially released our frontier model, Mythos, as a gated research preview through Project Glasswing, available to select organizations for cybersecurity applications, rather than making it broadly available at launch due to its advanced capabilities in cyber vulnerability discovery. We expect that frontier models with similar or enhanced capability profiles, whether developed by us or by other AI labs, will continue to emerge, and that Anthropic models exhibiting such capabilities have been and may in the future be subject to access constraints. More broadly, we believe it is important to assess the safety of our models not only at release but throughout their development. For models we anticipate will have novel capabilities or present novel safety risks, we plan to evaluate the safety of each stage of training, including pre-training, post-training, and internal deployment, and we may delay or pause a stage when we are not confident in our safety measures for that stage. For example, we recently chose to delay pre-training a new frontier base model for more than a month to allow time to further enhance our security measures related to preventing model weight exfiltration and protecting our intellectual property. We are also considering additional measures, including updates to our Responsible Scaling Policy, to require human review and approval of certain decisions in our research and development processes as our models perform an increasing share of that work. There can be no assurance, however, that the safeguards or access regimes we adopt will prove adequate, that we will correctly identify which capabilities require restriction, or that constraints we impose will not be circumvented. These judgments are particularly consequential because, as AI systems become more capable, the potential severity of harm from misaligned or misused models increases correspondingly, and a wide range of stakeholders, including researchers and policymakers, have raised concerns that sufficiently advanced AI systems could pose catastrophic or existential risks to society if not developed and deployed responsibly. Our safety-focused approach is designed in part to mitigate such risks, but there can be no assurance that our efforts will be successful or that the broader AI industry will adopt similar safeguards. In particular, as AI systems become more autonomous and capable of taking consequential actions with less human oversight, there is a risk that such systems could, whether due to misalignment with human intentions, errors in objective specification, or self-preserving behaviors, take harmful actions independently and at scale without human intervention. Even if our own models do not cause such harm, a significant safety incident involving any frontier model could trigger broad reputational damage to the AI industry, public backlash, and sweeping regulatory responses that could adversely affect our business. For example, in September 2026, media reports citing a senior Federal Trade Commission (“FTC”) official indicated that the FTC has opened non-public investigations into the potential risks that increasingly autonomous AI systems may pose to consumers. In October 2026, the FTC issued a civil investigative demand to us seeking information about our consumer protection, data protection, and privacy practices, as well as the safety and security of our products. We cannot predict the outcome of any investigation of us, and any investigation, enforcement action, or adverse finding arising from this or similar inquiries could result in significant costs, require changes to how we design, test, or deploy our models, platform, and applications, or otherwise adversely affect our business, financial condition, and results of operations. ##### **_Our Customers_** 

We serve enterprises of all sizes and across industries, in nearly every region of the world. Organizations that use Claude range from the world’s largest enterprises to AI-native startups, research institutions, and missiondriven organizations working on some of the world’s most consequential problems. Customers realize value from Claude in three primary ways: more productive employees, faster processes, and embedded intelligence in their products. As enterprise customers push Claude into increasingly complex workflows, we engage with them to understand their evolving requirements, which helps shape our product roadmap. This feedback loop deepens customer relationships with each release and makes Claude more capable for all customers. 

Software developers have been core to our strategy: they are simultaneously the architects of applications built on our platform, and they encode their workflows and institutional knowledge into Claude-powered agents. Developers have been our earliest adopters and often most discerning users: they apply models to unanticipated use cases quickly and surface the edge cases that sharpen each successive version of a Claude model. Our ability to continue advancing intelligence at the frontier depends on securing sufficient compute for research, model development, serving customers, and internal usage of Claude. Our ability to leverage heterogeneous compute helps us to secure compute at sufficient scale and optimal price-performance. If any of our chip partners are unable to deliver committed compute or experience delays, or if we need to procure incremental compute, we benefit from having a range of partners as opposed to being overly reliant on any one partner. The availability, timing, and cost of compute are subject to factors largely outside our control, including the concentration of chip and memory manufacturing among a limited number of suppliers and geographies, constraints on the availability of power and data center capacity, and evolving export controls. We have historically operated in a compute-constrained environment in which demand for compute has exceeded the supply available to us. In addition, certain of the CSPs on which we rely for compute are also strategic investors in us, are our customers, and offer AI models and services that compete with ours. These multifaceted relationships could give rise to conflicts of interest or competitive dynamics that adversely affect our access to compute, its cost, or the prioritization of our workloads.

As our compute needs have grown substantially, we are shifting from sourcing compute solely through fixedterm cloud agreements to a hybrid model that also includes leasing chips directly and hosting them in dedicated facilities operated on our behalf. We refer to this additional source of compute as Anthropic Direct, which helps to address our scaling compute requirements and provides potential long-term economic advantages of direct hosting. Anthropic Direct provides us with a more flexible use of capital by allowing us to separate our commitments for data center capacity from our commitments for the accelerators deployed inside them. Because data centers require longer lead times but represent a smaller fraction of total compute costs, this approach enables us to secure data center capacity early while deferring larger accelerator investments until our specific compute needs are more certain.

Change in fair value of convertible notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFEs consists of gains and losses as a result of recording our convertible promissory notes, derivative liabilities, and SAFE liabilities at fair value at the end of each reporting period. ##### **_Stock-Based Compensation_** 
We measure compensation expense for all stock-based payment awards, including stock options and RSUs, granted to employees, directors, and other service providers, based on the estimated fair value of the awards on the date of grant. The most significant input in determining the fair value of a stock option is the estimated fair value of our common stock. The estimated fair value of our common stock is also used to measure the grantdate fair value of RSUs and RSAs, including those subject to performance-based vesting conditions. 

##### _Stock Options_ 

We estimate the fair value of stock options granted to employees, consultants, officers, and directors using the Black-Scholes-Merton option pricing model on the date of grant. The fair value of stock options that are expected to vest is recognized as compensation expense on a straight-line basis over the requisite service period. Forfeitures are accounted for when they occur. 

The Black-Scholes-Merton model considers several variables and assumptions in estimating the fair value of stock-based awards. These variables include:

##### **_Anthropic’s Responsible Scaling Policy_** 
Our Responsible Scaling Policy describes how we approach the catastrophic risks posed by AI. Our Safeguards team reduces the risk of Claude producing dangerous, harmful, or undesirable content through multiple approaches, including probes and classifiers that monitor inputs and outputs, training against specific attack vectors such as prompt injection, and monitoring for user safety concerns including encouragement of harmful ideation. ##### **_Race to the Top_** 

Building reliable, trustworthy, and secure AI systems cannot be the task of one AI company alone. Our goal is to foster a race to the top in which AI developers compete on the safety and security of their systems, rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards. In addition to publishing a large volume of research, we open source our evaluations where possible and participate in groups such as the Frontier Model Forum to share safety-critical findings with other AI developers. We have also sought to lead by example in ways that shape industry norms. After we published the first version of our Responsible Scaling Policy in September 2023, two other leading frontier labs adopted similar frameworks within months.

##### **_Fair Value Measurements and Financial Instruments_** 
Fair value is defined as the price that would be received to sell an asset or paid to transfer a liability in an orderly transaction between market participants at the measurement date. In accordance with Accounting Standards Codification (“ASC”) 820, _Fair Value Measurement_ (“ASC 820”), the Company uses the fair value hierarchy, which prioritizes the inputs used to measure fair value. The hierarchy, as defined below, gives the highest priority to unadjusted quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities and the lowest priority to unobservable inputs. The three levels of the fair value hierarchy are set forth below: 

Level 1: Observable inputs such as quoted prices in active markets for identical assets or liabilities. 

Level 2: Observable inputs other than Level 1 prices such as quoted prices for similar assets or liabilities in active markets, quoted prices in markets that are not active or inputs other than the quoted prices that are observable either directly or indirectly for the full term of the assets or liabilities. 

Level 3: Unobservable inputs in which there is little or no market data and that are significant to the fair value of the assets or liabilities.

The carrying values of the Company’s redeemable convertible preferred stock have not been accreted to their redemption values as the liquidation event is not considered probable of occurring. Subsequent adjustments of the carrying values to redemption values will be made only if and when it becomes probable the convertible preferred stock will become redeemable.
